checkpoints: Keeping a rate limiter's remaining-token count on a private field of a service instance means every replica running behind a load balancer holds its own independent copy of that count, so the aggregate throughput allowed across all replicas is roughly N times the intended per-key limit.

In-memory counter state does not survive a process restart: a redeploy or crash-restart re-initializes the field to its starting capacity, silently resetting the limiter to full even though no time-based refill was actually earned.

Implementing a Redis-backed limiter as a plain `GET` followed by a plain `SET` is not atomic — the two calls are separate network round trips, so two concurrent requests can both read the same stored token count, both compute the same decremented value, and both write it back, losing one decrement and letting more requests through than the limit allows (a TOCTOU race).

The fix is to collapse the entire read-refill-decrement-write sequence into a single Lua script executed via Redis `EVAL`, because Redis runs each Lua script to completion on its single command thread, so no other client's command can interleave in the middle of the sequence.

The bucket must be keyed per logical entity being limited (for example `user:channel`) so that every replica reads and writes the same shared counter in Redis instead of each maintaining its own state, and the key should carry a TTL/expiry so an idle bucket is cleaned up automatically instead of accumulating in Redis forever.

Overshooting a provider's send-rate limit is a production-severity blocker rather than a style nitpick, because the sending IP or account can get throttled or blocked by the notification provider/carrier, taking down message delivery for the whole system.

This class of bug passes cleanly in a single-instance local or test environment because there is only one process and no real concurrent network round trip to expose the race — it only manifests once the service is actually scaled out to multiple replicas under concurrent load.

Verifying the fix requires a concurrency test: fire capacity-plus-one requests at the same key simultaneously (ideally from at least two separate instances or connections) and assert that exactly one request is rejected, which proves the counting is atomic and shared rather than racy or per-process.
